newsitem.title: USA: Albright says credibility at stake chemical pact.
newsitem.headline: Albright says credibility at stake chemical pact.

text.p: New Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Friday that a global chemical weapons ban soon to come into effect was "made in America" and that the United States risked losing credibility if the Senate failed to ratify it.

Albright promised an all-out effort to overcome Senate roadblocks to the treaty in her first policy speech since taking office on Jan. 23. The speech also strongly attacked isolationist trends in the United States and backed demands for an end to the steady decline in the State Department budget.

"Make no mistake, the Chemical Weapons Convention is in the best interests of the United States. In fact the CWC has 'made in America' written all over it," she said in the address at Houston's Rice University.
Conservative Republicans in the Senate say the 1993 treaty, which bans production, stockpiling and use of poison gas, has major flaws, and are holding up its ratification.

Unless Congress ratified the treaty by April 29, the date it enters into force, the United States would lose the right to administer the pact and risk the loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in chemical export sales, Albright said.

And, she said, "we would lose credibility in negotiating arms reduction agreements generally, because our ability to deliver in the Senate what we have proposed at the bargaining table would be undermined, for reasons that friends and allies around the world would find very difficult to understand."

President Bill Clinton, speaking in his annual State of the Union speech on Tuesday, called ratification of the treaty "a new test of leadership." He added: "It will make our troops safer from chemical attack. It will help us to fight terrorism."
But critics say it is difficult to verify, is not binding on states that have not signed it such as Iraq, Libya and North Korea, and will impose burdens on the U.S. chemical industry.

Part of Albright's aim in coming to Houston was to garner support from former President George Bush and former Secretary of State James Baker, both Texans and both Republicans who played a key role in negotiating the pact.

Baker, who preceded her on the platform at Rice, gave her the backing she was seeking, saying he supported the convention "for reasons that have nothing to do with domestic politics." She was due to meet Bush on Saturday.

Albright gained further backing at a meeting in Houston on Friday with Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria of Mexico, which has ratified the treaty. Gurria said Mexico was satisfied with administration efforts to overcome Senate hurdles.
Much of Albright's speech was devoted to lamenting the waning funding for U.S. foreign policy. "Diplomatically, we are steadily and unilaterally disarming ourselves," she said.

Her speech came the day after the Clinton administration in its annual budget presentation asked Congress for a seven percent rise for foreign operations which, if granted, would reverse a decade of declines.
Albright declared that "today, the greatest danger to America is not some foreign enemy; it is the possibility ... that we will succumb to the temptation of isolation."

The next decade or two would decide whether this generation had consolidated democracy or "allowed totalitarianism and fascism to rise again," whether Americans had deterred aggression or been "world class ditherers."
Despite the self-critical tone, Albright could not resist a swipe at America's European allies.
An American who bribed a foreign official to win a contract would be fined or sent to jail, she said. "If a European bribes that same foreign official, chances are he will get a tax deduction."
